title: THEY AGREED TO EAT THEIR OWN CHILDREN. THEN ONE MOTHER BROKE HER PROMISE—AND A KING TORE HIS CLOTHES.
paragraphs: THEY AGREED TO EAT THEIR OWN CHILDREN. THEN ONE MOTHER BROKE HER PROMISE—AND A KING TORE HIS CLOTHES.
The horrifying agreement inside a starving city, the mother's cry that exposed a nation's collapse, and the God whose mercy reaches into places human beings can barely bear to remember.
Based on 2 Kings 6:24–7:20 | A Gospel Warrior Reflection on Judgment, Human Desperation, Repentance, and the Grace of Jesus Christ
There are stories in the Bible that comfort you.
Stories that remind you God is faithful. Stories that make you close your eyes, breathe deeply, and whisper, “Thank You, Lord.”
And then there are stories that make your stomach turn.
Stories so disturbing that you wonder why God allowed them to be written down.
This is one of them.
Two mothers.
Two children.
A starving city.
And an agreement so horrifying that even the king, a man accustomed to violence and suffering, tore his royal garments when he heard what had happened.
But before you turn away, understand something.

This story is not merely about what starvation can do to the human body. It is about what happens when a broken world reaches the limits of human strength—and why our deepest hope cannot rest in human power.
Because somewhere beneath the horror of this ancient account is a question that still reaches into our lives today.
What happens when desperation becomes so overwhelming that the unthinkable begins to look like the only way out?
And where is God when people are suffering beyond what words can describe?
Stay with this story.
Not because its darkness deserves your fascination.
But because the darkness makes the need for redemption impossible to ignore.
The city was Samaria, the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.
Outside its walls stood the army of Ben-hadad, king of Aram, also called Syria in many English translations.
The enemy had surrounded the city.
Food supplies were running out.
The roads were blocked.
No ordinary family could simply walk into the countryside and gather grain.
And slowly, relentlessly, hunger began doing what armies sometimes could not.
It broke the people from within.
Second Kings 6:25 describes a famine so severe that a donkey's head sold for eighty shekels of silver, while a small measure of what the Hebrew text calls dove's dung sold for five shekels.

Even the exact identification of that second commodity has been debated by interpreters. What is unmistakable is the point of the passage: things ordinarily regarded as undesirable had become extraordinarily expensive.
The economy had collapsed into desperation.
Imagine a mother searching her home for something—anything—to feed her child.
An empty container.
A cold cooking fire.
A little one asking when they would eat again.
And no answer she could honestly give.
The Bible does not tell us the private thoughts of the women in this account.
It does not describe their homes, their childhoods, or how long they had been hungry.
We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But it tells us enough to understand that this was no ordinary hardship.
This was a city approaching the edge of human endurance.
Then came the moment that made even the king stop.
He was walking along the wall of Samaria when a woman cried out to him.
In the Hebrew text, her appeal begins:
הוֹשִׁיעָה אֲדֹנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ
Hoshi'ah, adoni ha-melekh.
“Help, my lord, O king.”
—2 Kings 6:26
That first word comes from the Hebrew root associated with saving or delivering.
She was asking for rescue.
And the king's response was bitter.
“If the LORD do not help thee, whence shall I help thee?”
—2 Kings 6:27, KJV
He spoke of the threshing floor and the winepress—the very places from which food and drink might ordinarily come.
But there was nothing left to distribute.
No royal decree could make grain appear.
No crown could fill an empty stomach.
And no political authority, however powerful, could simply command the siege to end.
Then the king asked what troubled her.
Perhaps he expected another complaint about food.
Perhaps another plea for relief.
But what she said was far worse.
“This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son to morrow.”
—2 Kings 6:28, KJV
Read those words again.
Not quickly.
Not as though they belong to a distant world that has nothing to say to ours.
Two women had made an agreement involving their own children.
The first woman's son was killed and eaten.
Then, when the next day came, the other woman hid her son.
And the first mother brought her complaint to the king.
The horror of the account is not simply that a terrible agreement was made.
It is that the woman presented the other mother's refusal to surrender her child as the injustice requiring royal intervention.
The moral world had become so distorted that a mother was asking the king to enforce an agreement that should never have existed.
The Bible records this without inviting us to enjoy the horror.
It does not ask us to admire either woman.
It does not give us permission to treat a murdered child as a mere illustration.
A real child, within the world of this narrative, had been destroyed.
And another child had been hidden.
We do not know whether the second mother's decision came from remorse, renewed maternal protection, fear, or some combination of motives.
The text does not tell us.
It simply tells us that she hid her son.
And sometimes the most responsible way to read Scripture is to let its silences remain silent.
But the king's response was visible to everyone.
When he heard the woman's words, he tore his clothes.
And beneath his royal garments, the people saw sackcloth.
In the ancient world, tearing one's garments was a recognized expression of grief, distress, or anguish.
Sackcloth was associated with mourning, humiliation, and sometimes repentance.
The king had already been wearing it beneath his clothes.
Something about the suffering of the city had affected him.
Yet there is an important distinction.
Being devastated by suffering is not the same thing as responding to God in faithful repentance.
Because what happened next reveals a king whose anguish turned toward blame.
In 2 Kings 6:31, he swore that Elisha the prophet would lose his head.
The narrative does not fully explain every motive behind his threat.
But it clearly shows his anger directed toward God's prophet.
Instead of giving us a simple portrait of a repentant ruler, Scripture presents a deeply troubled king whose response included violence.
And that should make us uncomfortable.
Because pain can bring people to their knees.
But pain can also make them search for someone to punish.
Some people become softer when life breaks them.
Others become harder.
Some cry out for mercy.
Others demand someone to blame.
And if we are willing to be honest, many of us have experienced both reactions within our own hearts.
Maybe you have never stood inside a besieged city.
Maybe you have never experienced hunger on anything approaching this scale.
But you know what it means to feel trapped.
To pray and wonder why the answer has not come.
To watch someone you love suffer while you feel powerless.
To become angry because the life you expected is not the life unfolding before you.
To ask God questions you are almost afraid to speak aloud.
“Lord, where are You?”
“Why has this happened?”
“How much longer?”
“Have You forgotten us?”
Those questions are not new.
They have echoed through generations of human suffering.
But there is something in this account that deserves our attention beyond the immediate tragedy.
Centuries before Samaria's siege, the covenant warnings given through Moses had described the terrible consequences that could accompany Israel's persistent rebellion.
Deuteronomy 28:53 warned that, under siege and extreme distress, people would eat the flesh of their own children.
Leviticus 26:29 contains a similarly horrifying warning.
These passages are not instructions.
They are not divine approval of cannibalism.
They are covenant warnings portraying the catastrophic consequences of judgment and siege.
Second Kings 6 depicts a tragedy that recalls those warnings with terrifying clarity.
This matters because the Bible is not presenting the event as an isolated example of human cruelty.
It belongs to a larger history of Israel's covenant unfaithfulness, national suffering, prophetic warning, and God's dealings with His people.
Yet we must also be careful.
Scripture does not authorize us to look at every starving family, every grieving parent, or every suffering child today and declare that their tragedy proves they personally sinned.
Jesus rejected that kind of simplistic judgment.
In Luke 13:1–5, He spoke about people who had suffered violent and sudden deaths. He did not teach that they were worse sinners than everyone else.
Instead, He called His hearers to examine their own need for repentance.
That is a crucial distinction.
The suffering of others is not an invitation for us to become their judges.
It is a reminder of the fragility of life, the seriousness of evil, and our desperate need for God.
And the child in Samaria must never disappear beneath our desire to draw a spiritual lesson.
That child's death was evil.
The mother's grief and guilt are not explained away by a sermon.
The king's torn clothes did not reverse what had happened.
And even the extraordinary deliverance that followed would not make that loss insignificant.
The Bible allows us to face that terrible reality.
But the story does not end on the city wall.
And this is where the account takes an astonishing turn.
While the king was threatening Elisha, the prophet announced a word from the LORD.
By the following day, food would be available at the gate of Samaria at dramatically reduced prices.
Read 2 Kings 7:1.
It was a promise that must have sounded almost impossible.
One day, famine.
The next, abundance.
One day, food beyond reach.
The next, ordinary provisions available again.
An officer who supported the king expressed disbelief.
Even if the LORD opened windows in heaven, he questioned whether such a thing could happen.
Elisha answered that the officer would see the promised provision but would not eat from it.
Then the narrative shifts away from the palace.
Away from the king.
Away from the powerful.
And toward four men with leprosy or a serious skin disease, sitting at the entrance of the city gate.
They were desperate too.
They reasoned that remaining where they were meant death.
Entering the starving city offered no hope.
So they decided to approach the Aramean camp.
And what they discovered was extraordinary.
The enemy had fled.
According to 2 Kings 7:6, the LORD had caused the Aramean army to hear the sound of chariots, horses, and a great army.
Believing an overwhelming military force was approaching, they abandoned their camp.
Their tents remained.
Their supplies remained.
Their food remained.
The four men entered, ate, drank, and began collecting valuables.
Then something changed.
They realized that keeping the discovery to themselves while an entire city starved was wrong.
In the King James Version, their confession is unforgettable:
“We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.”
—2 Kings 7:9
This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.
In Hebrew, the central expression is:
יוֹם־בְּשֹׂרָה הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה
Yom-besorah hayom hazzeh.
“This day is a day of good news.”
The word besorah refers to good news or a favorable report.
In its immediate context, it is news of deliverance from a military siege.
We should not pretend the verse was originally written as a direct prediction of the New Testament Gospel.
It was not.
But the language of good news creates a powerful biblical connection.
People facing death were told that deliverance had come.
People who believed they had no future discovered that the enemy had fled.
And those who found the provision recognized that the news was too important to keep to themselves.
Can you imagine?
Somewhere inside Samaria, parents were still looking at empty food containers.
Somewhere, people were wondering whether they would survive another day.
And outside the walls, food was waiting in an abandoned enemy camp.
They simply did not know it yet.
The four men carried the news back.
The king initially suspected a trap, but the report was investigated.
The abandoned camp was discovered.
And the people went out to obtain its provisions.
The word spoken through Elisha was fulfilled.
But the officer who had doubted the promise was trampled at the gate and died, just as the prophet had foretold.
Second Kings 7 does not end with a vague declaration that everything turned out perfectly for everyone.
It records provision, fulfilled prophecy, and judgment.
The starving city received relief.
Yet the murdered child did not return.
That is the tension we must not erase.
God's deliverance was real. So was the suffering that preceded it.
And now we come to the question that changes how a Christian reads this entire account.
Where is Jesus in a story like this?
We must answer carefully.
Jesus is not explicitly named in 2 Kings 6–7.
The passage is not secretly describing the crucifixion through every detail of the siege.
We should not turn the two mothers into invented symbols or force every character to represent someone in the New Testament.
But when we read the whole Bible as Christians, we see that this terrible account belongs to the larger story of humanity's need for redemption.
And that larger story leads us to Jesus Christ.
The siege reveals how deeply human life can be devastated by sin, violence, judgment, and desperation.
The king reveals the limits of earthly power.
The prophet's announcement reveals that deliverance ultimately came from the LORD.
And the four men reveal the moral urgency of sharing life-giving news.
Yet the Gospel announces something even greater than the lifting of an ancient siege.
It announces that Jesus Christ entered our fallen world to save sinners.
Not by pretending evil was harmless.
Not by calling darkness light.
Not by declaring repentance unnecessary.
But by bearing our sins and accomplishing the redemption we could never achieve for ourselves.
The apostle Paul wrote:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
—Romans 5:8, KJV
Notice those words.
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every mistake.
Not after we had made ourselves worthy.
Not after we had hidden every shameful chapter from view.
Christ died for sinners.
This does not mean every consequence of evil disappears in this life.
It does not mean victims must pretend their wounds never happened.
It does not mean forgiveness excuses abuse, cruelty, or injustice.
It means that the mercy of God in Christ is not reserved for people who can honestly claim they have never needed it.
And who among us could make that claim?
Some people reading this are carrying shame they have never confessed.
Not the horror of Samaria.
Perhaps something no one else knows.
A betrayal.
An addiction.
A relationship damaged by dishonesty.
A season of bitterness.
A choice that wounded someone.
Years spent resisting the voice of God.
You smile in public.
You answer messages.
You attend church.
You tell people you are doing fine.
But somewhere in the silence, you keep returning to the same question.
“Could God still forgive someone like me?”
Listen to the Gospel.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is not permission to continue in sin without repentance.
It is an invitation to stop hiding and come into the light.
And there is another truth we must remember.
Not everyone carrying pain is carrying guilt for what happened to them.
Some readers are not struggling because of something they did.
They are struggling because of something someone did to them.
If that is you, the Gospel does not demand that you accept blame for another person's wrongdoing.
Jesus sees the oppressed.
He cares for the wounded.
He calls His people to defend the vulnerable and practice justice.
And His grace is not limited to those who need forgiveness.
It is also hope for those who need healing.
Consider the difference between the king of Samaria and the King revealed in the Gospels.
The king of Samaria heard a woman's cry and was confronted by the limits of his power.
Jesus heard the cries of suffering people and responded with compassion.
He touched lepers.
He welcomed the rejected.
He fed hungry crowds.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He gave dignity to people others had dismissed.
And when He saw the multitudes, Matthew 9:36 tells us He was moved with compassion because they were distressed and scattered, like sheep without a shepherd.
The Greek word used there is:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
Esplanchnisthē.
It expresses being deeply moved with compassion.
Not distant politeness.
Not empty religious language.
Deep compassion.
And this is the Jesus we proclaim.
A Savior who does not delight in human misery.
A Savior who does not overlook sin.
A Savior who entered suffering, bore the cross, rose from the dead, and offers forgiveness and new life to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
The cross was not a decorative symbol of religious optimism.
It was the place where the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
And the resurrection was God's victorious declaration that death would not have the final word over Him.
This is why our hope is greater than the hope of Samaria.
Samaria needed food.
We need food too.
Hungry people must be fed, and Christians should never use spiritual language as an excuse to ignore physical suffering.
But humanity also needs reconciliation with God.
Jesus said:
“I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger; and he that believeth on me shall never thirst.”
—John 6:35, KJV
He was speaking of the life and satisfaction found in Him, not promising that His followers would never experience physical hunger.
His words invite us to recognize a need no earthly abundance can finally satisfy.
We need Him.
Not merely His blessings.
Not merely a solution to our immediate circumstances.
Not merely a religious identity that makes us look respectable.
We need Jesus Christ Himself.
And perhaps that is why this ancient account should disturb us so deeply.
Because it exposes the terrible things human beings can experience and do.
It strips away the illusion that civilization, wealth, authority, or religious appearance can save us from every form of evil.
It reminds us that earthly power has limits.
And it leaves us longing for a King whose righteousness cannot be corrupted and whose compassion cannot be exhausted.
That King is Jesus.
But there is something else in the story I cannot forget.
Those four men outside the city gate.
They found food.
They ate.
They discovered provision that could save lives.
Then they realized they could not remain silent.
“We do not well,” they said.
“This day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace.”
How many people around us are starving for hope while we remain silent about Christ?
Not everyone who looks successful is at peace.
Not everyone laughing is happy.
Not everyone posting beautiful family pictures has a healthy home.
Not everyone sitting in a church pew has surrendered their life to Jesus.
And not everyone who has walked away from church has stopped longing for God.
Some are wounded.
Some are skeptical.
Some are ashamed.
Some have questions they are afraid Christians will judge them for asking.
Some have heard religion their entire lives but have never clearly understood the Gospel of grace.
They need more than an argument.
They need truth spoken with love.
They need Christians whose lives reflect the Savior they proclaim.
They need to hear that repentance is possible, forgiveness is offered through Christ, and a new life can begin by His grace.
And sometimes that conversation begins with something as simple as sharing a message.
That is why I want to ask you something personal.
Who came to your mind while you were reading this?
A brother who has drifted from God?
A daughter who no longer prays?
A friend whose smile is hiding exhaustion?
A husband or wife who has become spiritually distant?
Someone who believes their past has disqualified them from ever coming back to Jesus?
Do not use this story to shame them.
Do not send it as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.
Sometimes love knows when to speak publicly.
And sometimes love knows when to protect someone's dignity.
If this message exposed something in your own heart, you do not have to pretend.
You do not need to reveal private wounds or painful details to prove your sincerity.
God already knows what you are carrying.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes, wondering whether you can still come home to Him, remember the words of Jesus:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.”
—John 6:37, KJV
What an extraordinary promise.
Come to Him.
Not to an image of yourself that you are trying to maintain.
Not to the reputation you are afraid to lose.
Not to the religious performance you think might impress Him.
Come to Jesus.
Confess your sins.
Trust in His death and resurrection.
Turn from the darkness that has been ruling your life.
And follow Him.
Grace does not mean sin was never serious.
Grace means Christ is a sufficient Savior.
And because He is alive, the past does not have to be the final author of your future.
This is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior.
Not because every earthly tragedy receives a happy ending before sunset.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
Not because faith guarantees a life without grief.
But because Jesus Christ has accomplished a redemption that sin, shame, and death cannot ultimately overthrow.
That is why we continue proclaiming the Gospel.
That is why we continue creating Scripture-centered articles, devotionals, books, and discipleship resources.
Gospel Warrior is not simply trying to produce more content.
Our desire is to help more people encounter the truth of Scripture, understand the Gospel, grow in discipleship, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
These resources are part of our commitment to make biblical encouragement and Christian learning accessible to people who may not otherwise have the means to obtain them.
Not because a payment can purchase spiritual favor.
Not because anyone should feel guilty for being unable to give.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
And Philippians 4:15–18 shows how believers financially partnered with Paul in Gospel ministry.
It should not be confused with a required biblical tithe or presented as a substitute for giving to your local church.
Rather, it is an additional opportunity to participate in Christian ministry as God leads and as your circumstances allow.
It is the opportunity to help keep biblical teaching and Gospel encouragement available to people who need them.
And if you have reached this far, I want to leave you with one final question.
Are you merely surviving spiritually, or are you truly following Jesus?
Because there is a difference.
You can know religious language and still be far from God.
You can recognize Bible stories and still resist the truth they reveal.
You can speak about grace while refusing to repent.
You can be surrounded by Christian content and still neglect prayer, Scripture, fellowship, and obedience.
But today, you can turn toward Christ.
Not tomorrow, when you think you will be more worthy.
Not someday, when your life finally looks presentable.
Today.
The God who brought deliverance to Samaria is the same God whose redemptive purposes find their fulfillment in Jesus Christ.
And the Gospel is not that we can somehow rescue ourselves if we become strong enough.
The Gospel is that Jesus came to save sinners.
So bring Him your guilt.
Bring Him your grief.
Bring Him the questions you cannot answer.
Bring Him the sins you need to confess.
Bring Him the brokenness you cannot repair by yourself.
And trust the Savior who died and rose again.
If you are ready to turn back to Him, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I need You. I confess that I have sinned and cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Forgive me, change my heart, and teach me to follow You. Give me the courage to turn away from sin and walk in Your truth. Heal what is wounded, correct what is wrong, and make my life a testimony of Your grace. Amen.”
Prayer is not a formula that earns salvation. Our hope rests in Jesus Christ, received through faith, not in the perfection of our words.
And if you prayed sincerely, do not let this be the end of your response.
Open your Bible.
Seek fellowship in a faithful local church.
Learn from mature believers.
Walk in repentance.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
The story of Samaria began with a city surrounded by death.
It showed us a mother crying to a king who could not save her child.
It showed us a ruler tearing his garments in anguish.
It showed us four desperate men discovering that good news was too important to keep to themselves.
And it leaves us with a choice.
We can read the account, feel disturbed, and move on.
Or we can allow it to remind us how desperately this world needs the righteousness, mercy, and redemption found in Jesus Christ.
Because the deepest answer to human darkness is not pretending the darkness never existed.
It is turning toward the Savior who entered our broken world and overcame death.
The king of Samaria tore his clothes when he heard how far humanity had fallen. But the King of kings gave His life to redeem sinners who could never lift themselves back up.
